transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-28
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 1h15m (approx)
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Maria Chen (Redwood SE), Daniel Ortega (CTO - Rivermark), Amira Khan (Lead Security Engineer), Ethan Rhodes (Network Architect), Samantha Li (Compliance Manager)

Summary (auto): Security deep dive focused on private VPC deployment and network-level controls, auditability, and key management. Agreed to exchange attestation docs and run an architecture mapping session.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: okay team thanks for joining, we'll do a deep dive into Redwood Private VPC and the security architecture, um Maria will cover network flows and I'll cover compliance bits, please interrupt with questions.
[00:12] Daniel Ortega: sounds good, quick note we want to make sure there are no public egress points and that we can manage keys in house, that's kind of top of mind.
[00:20] Maria Chen: yup, totally understood. we'll start with the control plane vs data plane separation — in our private offering the control plane can be managed by Redwood but it's possible to run the control plane in the customer's VPC for high security customers, or we provide a private control plane with customer-managed networking.
[00:34] Amira Khan: is that the same as the "Redwood Private VP C" option? sorry auto transcribe.
[00:38] Jordan Lee: yes, it's Redwood Private VPC — sometimes the transcript mangles it. so important part is the data plane nodes (the actual inference pods) live in your VPC without public IPs. Maria, can you walk flows?
[00:50] Maria Chen: sure, picture three subnets: management, serving, and storage. serving instances are in private subnets behind an internal load balancer (ILB). there are no inbound public routes. management access is via a bastion or customer-managed VPN/Direct Connect for ops. we support PrivateLink (AWS) / Private Endpoint (Azure) for APIs so your apps can hit endpoints privately.
[01:12] Ethan Rhodes: for management, do you require a NAT for egress to pull updates or do images get pushed? we want to avoid outbound internet if possible.
[01:20] Maria Chen: great question. we have two patterns: 1) customer-managed egress where the nodes use a NAT gateway and you control outbound IPs, or 2) air-gapped/on-prem option where images and updates are staged via an offline package. for cloud VPCs we can also support VPC endpoints to S3 and ECR so you never traverse public internet.
[01:40] Amira Khan: and firewalling — can we put upstream firewall appliances or next-gen FW between subnets? we want IDS/IPS and deep packet inspection on egress.
[01:48] Maria Chen: yes, we don't block that. standard deployment allows you to insert firewall appliances or virtual appliances into the egress path. security groups and NACLs are applied on the serving subnets; you can also route egress through a transit gateway with inspection.
[02:05] Jordan Lee: we often recommend routing egress through a customer-managed proxy so you can enforce filtering and TLS inspection if you need, and that gives you stable egress IPs for vendor allowlists.
[02:16] Samantha Li: can audit logs be forwarded to our SIEM? retention is a compliance requirement — we need 7 years for some logs.
[02:24] Maria Chen: yes, audit and request logs can be forwarded in near-real time. we support pushing logs to your CloudWatch/Stackdriver/Log Analytics, or syslog to a collector, or direct ingestion into Splunk/Datadog via an agent. retention is configurable; Redwood's default retention is shorter but for Private we can arrange longer retention or streaming to your storage for long-term retention.
[02:45] Daniel Ortega: encryption details — we must use customer-managed keys and HSM, FIPS 140-2. what's your KMS story?
[02:53] Jordan Lee: Redwood supports BYOK (bring your own key) patterns. in AWS we can use your CMKs in KMS or a dedicated Cloud HSM. for Azure we support Azure Key Vault with customer-managed keys. keys are used for disk encryption and for encrypting backups. we also support envelope encryption so customer CMK only wraps the data keys.
[03:15] Amira Khan: key rotation and access controls — how do we audit key usage?
[03:20] Maria Chen: we log CMK usage via CloudTrail or equivalent; we can export those logs into your SIEM. access to KMS is controlled by IAM roles that are mapped to the Redwood service account in your account, or in some cases via a customer-managed service role. rotation policy can be automated by your KMS.
[03:36] Ethan Rhodes: network-level TLS — is it mutual TLS between our app and the Private endpoint?
[03:40] Maria Chen: we support TLS and can enable mTLS for client connections. for API traffic over PrivateLink, you can configure TLS termination at the ILB and optionally require client certs.
[03:50] Daniel Ortega: how about RBAC and SSO — we use Okta and need SCIM provisioning and SAML SSO plus role mapping to our internal teams.
[03:58] Jordan Lee: we integrate with Okta, Azure AD, and other SAML providers. SCIM provisioning for users and groups is supported; RBAC in Redwood maps groups to roles (admin, ops, viewer, etc.). we also provide audit trails for user activity.
[04:12] Samantha Li: SOC two and ISO — do you have attestations? are there any gaps we should be aware of?
[04:18] Jordan Lee: we have SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 reports for the control plane and hosted offerings. for Private deployments we can provide the same attestations plus architecture diagrams and evidence of encryption/configuration. i'll share a redacted attestation pack after the call.
[04:32] Amira Khan: does SOC 2 cover the private deployment when the control plane is customer-managed?
[04:36] Jordan Lee: if the control plane is customer-managed, the responsibilities split changes — we'll provide a control-mapping document that maps our controls to yours and highlight where evidence is customer-responsible. Maria will attach that mapping.
[04:48] Ethan Rhodes: practical question: do nodes need public IPs for health checks? we've seen services require outbound health pings.
[04:55] Maria Chen: no, health checks can be internal. any required external checks can be proxied through your monitoring stack. we avoid requiring public IPs.
[05:05] Daniel Ortega: patching and maintenance windows — how are these handled for Private?
[05:09] Maria Chen: for Private you control maintenance windows; we can coordinate with your ops. for Dedicated or hosted we have scheduled maintenance; for Private we either push patches through your pipeline or we provide the artifacts for you to patch.
[05:19] Amira Khan: SIEM integration again — format: do you send JSON logs, CEF, or syslog?
[05:24] Maria Chen: we support multiple formats: JSON over HTTPS, syslog, or we can write to an S3 bucket in structured JSON for ingestion. we recommend encrypted transport and signing if you need tamper-evidence.
[05:36] Jordan Lee: another operational control is network allowlisting. we can provide a set of egress IPs if you choose Redwood-managed egress, or you can pin egress via NAT in your account.
[05:46] Ethan Rhodes: can we run the inference nodes in our own K8s cluster on-prem?
[05:50] Maria Chen: yes, we have an on-prem package that runs in your datacenter; it uses the same runtime but packaged as a deployable appliance. in that model you own networking, and Redwood provides the management tooling and observability connectors.
[06:05] Amira Khan: when on-prem, do you still need connectivity back to Redwood for telemetry?
[06:09] Jordan Lee: telemetry is optional. we can push metrics to your Prometheus or you can let Redwood ingest telemetry over a customer-controlled egress channel. if you prefer fully air-gapped, we can operate without telemetry but feature sets for remote support differ.
[06:22] Samantha Li: one compliance question: do you support immutable logs / WORM for audit trails?
[06:27] Maria Chen: we can export logs to an immutable storage tier for retention (e.g., S3 with Object Lock) or push to your GCS with retention policies. we also support digest signing if you want tamper-evidence.
[06:40] Daniel Ortega: liability and data residency — our data cannot leave region. can you guarantee region-locked storage and processing?
[06:47] Jordan Lee: yes, we support region isolation. for Private we deploy entirely within the customer's region and do not replicate outside unless explicitly configured. we'll note region in the contract and mapping doc.
[06:58] Amira Khan: how do we validate the network topology? we'd like a runbook or template.
[07:02] Maria Chen: Maria: we'll share a VPC architecture diagram and a runbook that includes security group rules, NACL examples, NAT/proxy routing, and PrivateLink endpoints. also include example IAM policies and KMS key policies.
[07:18] Ethan Rhodes: can you provide sample firewall rules for vendor access and allowlisting?
[07:22] Maria Chen: yes, we'll provide sample security group ingress/egress, recommended NACLs, and a sample transit gateway routing table for inspection appliances.
[07:30] Jordan Lee: ok let's surface known risks: 1) split responsibility for control plane if customer manages it; 2) ensuring egress is controlled and inspected; 3) key management complexity if using BYOK. We'll provide mitigation docs for each.
[07:45] Amira Khan: one last point — we need proof of penetration testing and vulnerability scans. do you publish a pen test summary?
[07:51] Jordan Lee: we have red-team and pen-test reports for the runtime; we can provide an executive summary and scope under NDA. we'll add that to the materials.
[07:59] Daniel Ortega: great, thanks. next steps?
[08:03] Jordan Lee: recap — Jordan to share SOC2/ISO pack and pen-test summary, Maria to send VPC runbook and diagram plus sample PrivateLink config, Ethan/Amira to send egress IP and retention constraints. we'll schedule network mapping session week of 4/6.
[08:16] Samantha Li: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[08:20] Jordan Lee: thanks all, we'll follow up in email. bye.

Notes on transcription: occasional speaker labels and product names may be slightly off due to auto transcription (e.g., "VP C" instead of VPC). timestamps approximate.
